bp: Search engines learn from clicks because clicks are abundant and cheap. But a click is not a clean statement that a document was the best answer. A result near the top is more likely to be seen, and therefore more likely to be clicked, even when a lower result is equally relevant or better. Unbiased learning to rank tries to repair that measurement problem: it wants to learn the document's real usefulness while separating away the extra lift caused by position on the page. This paper asks a prior question that is easy to ignore: can the data actually support that separation? In a two-tower model, one side represents relevance and another represents position bias. The promise is that clicks can teach both. The danger is that the same clicks may be explainable by many different mixtures of relevance and position bias.
wh: The hard part is that relevance and position bias are tangled in the same observed event. A user either clicked or did not click; the log does not directly say whether the click happened because the document answered the query or because it appeared in an easy-to-see slot. If the same document, or a document with similar features, appears in many different positions, the system gets a useful comparison: what changes when position changes but the document is roughly the same? Existing theory says this can identify the two parts in the limit of endless data. Real logs are less generous. Some documents rarely move positions, some features do not overlap across positions, and sample sizes can be small for particular parameters. Then a model may fit clicks well while still leaving some bias parameters free to drift without being pinned down by evidence.
naive: A smart beginner would train the two-tower ranking model, check whether click prediction is accurate, and assume the learned relevance and position-bias values are trustworthy. That fails because good prediction does not guarantee unique explanation. Two different settings can predict the same clicks: one can say the top position is very attractive and the document is only moderately relevant; another can say the top position matters less and the document is very relevant. If both stories fit the observed clicks, the model has not really learned the separate causes. It has only found one convenient explanation among several equally plausible ones.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn identifiability into a practical stress test. Instead of asking only whether a trained model predicts clicks, it asks whether each individual bias parameter is forced by the data. The diagnostic takes a parameter at its best learned value, deliberately shifts it away, retrains the parts of the model that are allowed to compensate, and checks whether click-prediction performance gets meaningfully worse. If performance drops, the data objected to that shift; the parameter was constrained. If performance barely changes, the model found another way to explain the clicks, so that parameter was not uniquely determined. This changes identifiability from an infinite-data theorem into an empirical question about the actual log, logging policy, feature overlap, and sample size in front of the practitioner.
mech: The mechanism starts with a click dataset from a ranking system. Each record carries the displayed document, its position, and whether the user clicked. A two-tower model is trained to explain those clicks by combining a relevance part, tied to query-document information, with a position-bias part, tied to where the result appeared. After fitting the model, the diagnostic selects one bias parameter, such as the parameter for a particular position. It moves that parameter away from the value found during training. The rest of the model is then retrained or adjusted so it has a fair chance to recover click-prediction performance under the forced change. The diagnostic compares the new prediction loss with the original loss. A clear loss increase means the data could not absorb the artificial shift; that parameter is identified in the practical sense tested here. A flat loss curve means the model can compensate elsewhere, so the parameter is not pinned down. Repeating this for individual bias parameters builds a map of which parts of the bias model are supported. Simulations then vary logging randomness, feature overlap, and sample size to separate structural failures from failures caused by too little data.
math: The central mathematical idea is identifiability, which means uniqueness of explanation. If a clock shows noon, many hidden mechanisms could have produced that reading unless the observations rule all but one out. Here the visible reading is the click log, and the hidden mechanisms are relevance and position bias. A parameter is identifiable when changing it necessarily worsens the model's ability to account for the observed clicks after every allowed adjustment elsewhere. The second idea is loss minimization, which means defining a number that counts prediction error and choosing model settings that make that number small. The diagnostic studies the shape of that error number around a parameter. If the error rises when the parameter is moved, the data creates a valley with a real bottom. If the error stays nearly flat, the parameter lies on a plateau where many settings explain the clicks equally well. The paper also uses comparison logic: same or similar documents appearing across positions create the contrast needed to separate document appeal from position advantage. The tradeoff is reliability versus convenience: a model can be convenient to fit while its internal parts remain underdetermined.
dots: This paper sits inside information retrieval and search, but its deeper theme is separating cause from coincidence in logged behavior. Click logs are also used by recommendation, advertising, and personalization systems, and all face the same danger: observed action is shaped by both user preference and the platform's previous decision about what to show. It also connects to ranking because the learned model is not merely predicting clicks; it is supposed to produce a better ordering of documents once position effects are removed. The diagnostic resembles broader conference ideas about testing whether a learned score is actually constrained by evidence rather than just tuned to a dataset. Neighboring two-tower papers often focus on speed and matching quality. This one focuses on trust: before using a fast architecture to correct bias, ask whether the data contains enough variation for the correction to mean anything.
ww: The diagnostic works because unidentified parameters have a distinctive behavior: they can move without changing what the model says about the observed clicks. If the data never shows enough variation to distinguish two explanations, retraining can hide a forced change by adjusting other parts of the model. That is not a small numerical accident; it is evidence that the dataset does not contain the comparison needed to decide. Identified parameters behave differently. Their values are tied to actual contrasts in the log, such as documents or similar feature patterns appearing at different positions. When such a parameter is shifted, the model loses an explanation that the other parts cannot fully replace, so prediction error rises. The test is useful because it measures sensitivity in the finite dataset instead of assuming endless examples. It can also distinguish several failure sources: a modeling assumption may be wrong, the logging policy may not move documents enough, or there may simply be too few samples to expose the constraint.
po: The payoff is a diagnostic tool for practitioners who use two-tower models to correct position bias in learning to rank. It tells them which bias parameters are actually determined by their data and which can vary without hurting click prediction. The abstract reports simulations showing how non-deterministic logging policies, feature overlap, and larger samples affect identifiability. It also reports a real-world application to Baidu-ULTR where some parameters remain unidentified despite large click data. The practical benefit is avoiding false confidence: a system can predict clicks while still failing to learn the bias correction it claims to learn.
limits: The method assumes that prediction loss is a meaningful test of whether a shifted parameter has damaged the model's explanation of clicks. It also depends on how retraining is done after a shift; if the retraining procedure is weak, a parameter might look identified because the model failed to compensate. The abstract establishes simulations and one real dataset application, but it does not prove that every logging environment, query mix, or two-tower design will behave the same way. The diagnostic can reveal that a parameter is not pinned down; by itself, it does not create the missing positional variation or prove that learned relevance is correct.
